turns.text: Can you describe your first night after arriving in Beidahuang? What did you see, hear, and feel as you settled in?

The train left us at a platform that barely deserved the name, and the rest was a blur of mud and shouting. My boots, new from Shanghai, sank deep with each step. I remember the cold most — not the sharp kind that stings, but a damp, heavy cold that pressed through my coat and into my bones. The sky was huge, empty, and the wind moved across the land with nothing to block it. Inside the dormitory, the air smelled of wet straw and unwashed bodies. The walls were thin, patched with old newspapers, and I could hear every cough, every shift on the narrow beds. I lay awake, listening to the wind rattle the window and the unfamiliar breathing of girls I barely knew. My stomach gnawed at itself, half from hunger, half from worry. I thought of home, the noise of the city, the warmth of my sisters sleeping close by, and I realized how far I had come — not just in distance, but in the way the world could change overnight. I did not sleep. I stared at the ceiling until morning, afraid to close my eyes and wake up somewhere even colder.

Your memory of the cold and the strangeness of the dormitory really stands out. I’m struck by the detail about the walls patched with newspapers and the sounds of people you didn’t know. When you lay there that night, was there a moment when you tried to comfort yourself—maybe with something familiar from home, or a thought that helped you get through those first hours?

I remember clutching the little cloth pouch my mother had sewn for me, stuffed with dried orange peel and a few hairpins. The scent of the peel, faint and sweet, reminded me of winter evenings at home when we would sit around the coal stove, peeling fruit and listening to the radio. I pressed it to my nose under the blanket, trying to blot out the smell of straw and sweat. For a moment, I imagined I was back in our apartment, the walls close and safe, my mother’s voice drifting in from the kitchen. It was a small comfort, but it kept me from crying. I told myself I would write a letter home as soon as I could, even though I didn’t know what to say yet. That promise — to write, to keep a thread to my old life — helped me feel less lost.

The pouch became my anchor in those first weeks. I kept it hidden beneath my pillow, afraid someone might take it or tease me if they saw how tightly I clung to it. At night, when the others were asleep, I would turn my face to the wall and breathe in the orange scent, letting it fill my lungs until the ache in my chest softened. Sometimes I’d run my fingers over the stitches, tracing the pattern my mother’s hands had made. During the day, I tried to carry myself like I belonged there, but the pouch was my secret, a reminder that I hadn’t always been just another body in a line of workers. It was strange how something so small could hold back the loneliness for a while. The promise to write home became a ritual — I’d form the words in my head, even before I found paper, rehearsing what I could say without making my mother worry too much. That careful balance, between truth and comfort, became its own kind of burden.

Your description of rehearsing letters in your mind, trying not to worry your mother, makes me think about how isolating it must have felt to carry those unspoken truths. When you finally did find paper and wrote your first letter, do you remember what details you chose to include or leave out, and how you decided what your family should know?

I remember sitting at the edge of my bunk, hunched over a scrap of rough paper I’d managed to trade for a piece of hard candy. My hand shook as I wrote, partly from the cold, partly from the feeling that every word mattered. I told my mother that the journey had been long, but I was safe. I described the vast fields and the “fresh air,” though I left out how the wind cut through my coat and made my nose bleed. I mentioned that I was learning to cook simple meals with the other girls, but didn’t say that our rice was often gritty and our hands raw from scrubbing pots. I wrote that the people were “friendly,” though most of us barely spoke outside of work. I wanted her to picture me as capable, adjusting, even a little bit brave. I could not bring myself to write about the hunger or the way my Shanghai accent set me apart. I signed it with a joke about my clumsy boots, hoping she would smile. After sealing the letter, I lay awake, wondering if she would read between the lines and sense what I couldn’t say.

The act of writing that letter felt like walking a tightrope. Each sentence was weighed, measured, then rewritten in my head before it ever reached the page. I remember pressing the pencil so hard the tip snapped, and for a moment I just stared at the broken lead, thinking how easily things could split apart. I left out anything that hinted at despair — the cold that seeped into my bones, the silence at night, the ache in my legs that made me feel twice my age. I wanted to protect my family from worry, but I also needed them to believe I was still myself, not someone swallowed by hardship. Even the joke about my boots was a shield. I knew my mother would read it again and again, searching for clues. I wondered if she would hear the things I’d left unsaid, or if she would take comfort in the picture I painted, and I didn’t know which would be kinder.

The image of the pencil tip snapping as you wrote really lingers with me—it feels like a physical sign of how much you were holding in. You mentioned the ache in your legs and feeling twice your age; was there a particular day or task in those first weeks that made you especially aware of how different this life was from Shanghai?

There was a morning when we were sent out before sunrise to dig ditches along the edge of a frozen field. My hands, soft from city life, blistered and bled against the wooden handle of the shovel. The earth was hard as iron, and each time I drove the blade down, the shock traveled up my arms and rattled my teeth. My breath came out in clouds, mixing with the steam from the others as we worked in silence. I remember glancing down at my fingers, swollen and cracked, and thinking how I’d never even peeled a potato back home, let alone broken the earth. By midday, my legs felt hollow, as if the cold had eaten away the muscle. That night, I tried to scrub the dirt from my nails, but it was ground in too deep. I stared at my hands and realized they were changing — becoming rough, foreign, no longer the hands of a schoolgirl. That was when the distance from Shanghai felt most real: not just a place I’d left, but a self I couldn’t get back.

I can still feel the sting of that cold metal through my gloves, the numbness creeping up my arms until I couldn’t tell if I was gripping the shovel or if it was gripping me. The silence between us was heavy, broken only by the scrape and thud of blades hitting frozen ground. In Shanghai, my hands had been soft, my days measured by bells and lessons, not by how many meters of ditch I could finish before dusk. That day, the ache in my legs was sharp, but what stayed with me was the way my body started to feel like someone else’s — heavier, slower, marked by bruises and calluses. I remember thinking that no matter how hard I scrubbed, the dirt and ache would stay. I wondered if my mother would recognize me if she saw my hands, or if she would think I belonged to the fields now, not to her.

Your worry that your mother might not recognize your hands anymore is so powerful—it’s like your whole identity was shifting with your body. In those moments, did you ever talk about this sense of loss or change with the other girls in your dorm, or was it something everyone kept hidden?

We almost never spoke about it directly. At night, after lights out, there were sometimes whispers — a sigh about missing home, or a quiet complaint about aching feet. But mostly, we kept our feelings tucked away, like contraband. It felt dangerous to admit how lost we were, as if saying it out loud might make it worse, or mark you as weak. I remember once, while washing our hands in icy water, another girl glanced at her palms and muttered, “These aren’t mine.” We all heard, but no one answered. We just looked down and kept scrubbing. It was as if we had an unspoken agreement: we would survive by pretending we were getting used to it, even if we weren’t.

That silence between us was sometimes heavier than the work itself. If someone cried at night, the rest of us would turn away, pretending not to notice. Showing that kind of softness could make you a target, not just for ridicule, but for suspicion. I learned to swallow my words, to nod along when others joked about becoming “real peasants,” even though the joke tasted bitter. Sometimes I wanted to reach out, to ask if anyone else felt themselves disappearing, but I never did. The fear of standing out, of being seen as fragile or unwilling, was stronger than the urge to share. I think we all carried our losses in private, letting them settle in our bodies and our silences, because that was safer than letting them show.

The idea of carrying your losses in silence, letting them settle in your body, really stays with me. Looking back now, do you think that kind of silence and pretending changed how you understood friendship or trust, both then and later in your life?
